catalog_quote: 4.3 Stress Stress in words of Mongolic origin is ultimate in Santa. In other words, stress always falls on the last syllable of any given word. ... When a suffix is added, the stress normally shifts to the last syllable of the word. ... This is the default situation. (462) kuŋ-ˈla 'people' (kuŋ 'person' + -la 'PL') ... However, there is a small set of markers that do not cause the stress to shift when they are added. These are preceded by the symbol '='. ... In addition to these, there are two disyllabic suffixes which only cause the stress to shift to the first syllable of the disyllabic suffix when they are added. ... There are only a couple of words of Mongolic origin which are exceptions to the Santa ultimate stress pattern. (465) 'basi 'tiger' ... 'bosi 'cloth' ... new_statements.quote: p. 35: Word-final accent is shared by all QG languages. [...] In Dongxiang exceptions may occur in words whose last vowel has ended up in the penultimate syllable due to epenthesis, e.g. ˈbasï ‘tiger’ < *bars, ˈbosï ‘fabric’ < *bös. Loanwords from Arabic may have non-final accent, e.g. ˈsaχari ‘early morning meal’ from Arabic saħar, ˈaġili ‘intellect’ from Arabic ʕaql. Exceptions are also seen in Chinese loanwords, where non-final accents are perhaps the result of attempts to deal with tonal differences, and prevent homophony, e.g. Dgx ʂïˈʒï < shīzi ‘lion’ as opposed to ˈʂïʒï < shìzi ‘persimmon’. | p. 63: In the Shirongol languages the accent normally falls on the last syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (final: final stress). Adds the exception classes (epenthetic final vowels, Arabic and Chinese loans) and the reduction of unaccented vowels; also notes that Dongxiang is the most conservative QG language in vowel preservation. The bibliography (p. 27367 of dump) lists a dedicated study not opened here: Nasunbayar 1988, Dōngxiāngyŭde cízhòngyīn [Stress in Dongxiang], Dōngxiāngyŭ lùnjí, Lanzhou, 92-101 (Chinese, no open copy known).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the last syllable of the stem in Dongxiang, as in all Qinghai-Gansu (Shirongol) Mongolic languages; unaccented (mostly first and medial) vowels are reduced, though Dongxiang is the most conservative QG language in preserving them (p. 63, p. 92). Vowels added by epenthesis after a former final consonant do not take the accent, so the accent then sits on the historical last vowel, now penultimate (p. 35, fn. 278 p. 210: 'Note that in Dongxiang the added final vowels do not take the accent, e.g. ˈbosï < *bös'); connective vowels reanalysed as stem-final in verbs do take the accent (fn. 12, p. 35; p. 95 Dgx qïri- < *gar-).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Epenthetic final vowels after original final consonants are unaccented: ˈbasï 'tiger' < *bars, ˈbosï 'fabric' < *bös; fn. 12 says this 'may be more common than is indicated in the sources' (bosï < *boas 'pregnant' would be expected to have initial stress but is not so marked). (b) Arabic loans with non-final accent: ˈsaχari 'early morning meal', ˈaġili 'intellect'. (c) Chinese loans where a non-final accent keeps tonal minimal pairs apart: ʂïˈʒï 'lion' (shīzi) vs ˈʂïʒï 'persimmon' (shìzi), citing Bökh's dictionary and Liu (1981:17). Nugteren's Dongxiang data are from Bökh et al. 1983 and Liu 1981 (p. 27 area, line 969 of the text dump).
new_statements.identity_note: Nugteren treats Dongxiang (= Santa, Dgx) as a Baoanic/Shirongol Qinghai-Gansu Mongolic language; his Dongxiang forms come from Bökh et al. 1983 and Liu Zhaoxiong 1981 (the standard Chinese descriptions, presumably the Suonanba-based standard variety; no dialect is named). The p. 35 statement is about the QG group as a whole with Dongxiang-specific exceptions given explicitly; the p. 63 statement covers 'the Shirongol languages', which include Dongxiang.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed final stress in native vocabulary, rightward shift onto suffixes, a listed set of non-shifting clitics and two disyllabic suffixes, lexical exceptions in loans, explicitly weight-blind) rests on a dedicated stress section of the best available grammar (Field 1997, 463-pp UCSB dissertation), which we hold; the quotation was re-verified verbatim against scanned of the page images we hold at the stated pages (151-154 = PDF 184-187), and the held Nugteren 2011 monograph independently confirms word-final accent for Dongxiang with the same exceptions (ˈbasï, ˈbosï, Arabic and Chinese loans). The one open item downloaded now (Wu 1994, SPP 55) is silent on stress. Remaining unheld works (Kim 2003 sketch, Liu 1981, Nasunbayar 1981, Todaeva 1961) are older, shorter, or in Chinese/Mongolian/Russian and are unlikely to change the classification; at most Nasunbayar 1981 might add a secondary-stress r
